tenders.title: Tender board
tenders.intro: Tenders are decided at the end of their deadline quarter and start the quarter after. Green seats you can staff yourself, yellow partly. The rest is covered first by free people from other disciplines (flex, slightly lower rate), then by freelancers. Small gigs (1–2 consultants) appear every quarter. Key tenders (frameworks and big projects) come with a customer meeting and a promise about the start. Routine ones go out as a standard offer with one click.

tenders.lastChance: Last chance: decided when you end the quarter!

goal.title: Ten years, one quarter at a time
goal.body: You've just founded {{firm}}. You have {{quarters}} quarters, from {{start}} to {{end}}, to build the most valuable consultancy in the country. {{rivals}} other firms have the same idea.
points: Your firm's value is last year's operating profit times a multiple that follows your reputation, plus the cash in the bank.
Whoever is worth the most when time runs out wins.
Stay over your credit limit for too long and the firm goes bankrupt, which ends the game. However nice your slides were.

quarter.title: How a quarter works
quarter.body: Each turn is one quarter. Do as much as you like, then press “{{endTurn}}”. Your rivals make their moves and the books are settled.
points: Post job openings under {{staff}}. Whoever says yes starts the quarter after.
Work you win shows up under {{contracts}}. That's where the money comes from.
The to-do list on the {{dashboard}} shows what needs doing before the quarter ends.

tenders.title: Tenders take time
tenders.body: You can bid on a tender in the quarter it's published and the one after. The client decides at the end of that second quarter, and the work starts the quarter after that.
points: You need enough people in the right disciplines when the work starts, so hire a little ahead.
The customer weighs price against quality. Big tenders and frameworks come with a meeting and a promise about the start. Small jobs go out with one click.
When a contract is about to end, a happy client may renew it.

people.title: You sell people
people.body: Your consultants are the only thing you have to sell. People on the bench cost salary and earn nothing. People who work too hard leave.
points: The capacity panel on the {{dashboard}} shows who's billing and who's on the bench, now and next quarter.
Happy clients build your reputation, and reputation makes the firm worth more.
Morale keeps people around. Replacing a senior takes longer than you think.

ahead.title: What's ahead
ahead.body: The firm goes up a level when you hit any one of the goals for headcount, revenue or tenders won. Every level means a new office, bigger tenders and new options:

game.title: What is this?
body: Konsulent Tycoon is a turn-based strategy game where you run your own IT consultancy. You have {{quarters}} quarters, from {{start}} to {{end}}, to build the most valuable firm in the country. The only problem: {{rivals}} rivals had the exact same idea.

You hire people, bid on tenders, keep clients happy and try not to run out of cash. Whoever ends up with the most valuable firm when time runs out wins. Stay over your credit line for too long and you go bankrupt. That's life.

creator.title: Who made it?
body: That would be me! I'm Kristofer Giltvedt Selbekk, and I've worked at Bekk since 2013. I'm pretty proud of that, to be honest.

I've always loved tycoon games, especially Transport Tycoon, Theme Hospital and Theme Park. So I wanted to make something in the same spirit, set in an industry I know from the inside. Consulting, after all, is interesting, complex, fun and hard. All at once.

satire.title: How much of it is true?
body: Not much, thankfully. The game plays with common misconceptions and prejudices about what consultancies actually do. I've personally never met anything but thoroughly professional people in the industry, but there are plenty of prejudices to have fun with.
Every firm name is made up. If some of them remind you of my own employer and its competitors… that's mostly for fun.

making.title: How it was made
body: I built the game with Claude Code, lots of user testing and a whole lot of trial and error. Much like every other product I work on, really. The difference is that it took far less time than anything I have built before.

The background music was made with Claude Opus 5.5 too: 20 little tunes written as chords and style, with the melodies made by code and played by a synth right in your browser. Pretty neat, if you ask me.
The game is still in development, so things will change along the way. Keep an eye on News to see what's new.

privacy.title: Your data
body: The game is free and runs in your browser. Saved games stay on your own device and aren't sent anywhere. In short: I'd like to know how the game is played, but not who you are.

If you say yes to usage statistics, the game sends anonymous events to PostHog, on servers in the EU: which screens you open, what you do in the game (like bids, hires and crisis choices), how your quarters go, and error reports if something crashes. PostHog also gets what your browser shares about itself anyway, like browser, operating system, screen size, rough country and which page sent you here. I store a random ID on your device so I can tell it's the same player next time, and each game gets a random ID of its own too. I don't store your IP address, and I never send your firm's name or anything else you type.
If you say no, PostHog isn't loaded at all. You can change your mind at any time in Settings. If you play offline, events are sent once you're back online, as long as the game is still open.

If you join the leaderboard, the game sends that week's game to Firebase (Google), with servers in the EU. It stores an anonymous account (a random ID), the moves you made in the game, the result and the name you picked from the word list. Your firm name is not sent. This only happens when you press "Send it in" yourself, and you can delete the account and everything stored in Settings.

thanks.title: Thanks

bugs.title: Found a bug?

The code is open on GitHub. Feel free to open an issue with what happened and what you expected to happen, and I'll take a look. And if you feel like fixing it yourself, pull requests are more than welcome!

finance.title: New tab: Finance
body: Running a consultancy involves a lot of strange things, but at the end of the day it’s about money. How much comes in, how much goes out, and how long you can hold on when the first number is smaller than the second. Those numbers finally have a tab of their own: Finance. You’ll find it right after Overview.

At the top is this quarter’s budget, line by line. Salaries, office and running costs, culture, freelancers and partnerships, and most of them come with a shortcut to the tab where you actually get to change them. Next to it you’ll find your cash, credit line, burn rate and runway. Runway counts down to your credit limit, not to zero, because that’s where the bank starts getting uncomfortable. So zero in the account isn’t the end of the world. A bit below, though…

Further down you’ll find the accounts for each quarter, and from level 2 there are charts too, for cash, company value, revenue, result, utilisation and headcount going back three years. In the accounts you’ll meet a line called “other items”. It’s everything that moves money outside day-to-day operations: interest, fines, events and acquisitions. If you’ve ever wondered where all the money went, that’s probably your answer.

The Overview has slimmed down a little as a result. “This quarter” now only shows your result, value and rank, with a button through to Finance. And since the new tab took second place, the keyboard shortcuts for the other tabs have moved up by one. Sorry, muscle memory! Cheers!

welcome.title: Welcome to the news feed!
body: Hi, and welcome! This is the news section of Konsulent Tycoon, the place where I'll tell you what's going on with the game. Not in quarterly report form, mind you. That's your firm's job.

The game is still in active development (read: not even in beta), and there's a lot going on under the hood all the time. New crises, new minigames, and a never-ending hunt for balance between you and 24 rivals who would love to run off with your clients. Until now, most of it has happened in silence. Which is kind of a shame, if you ask me.

So what's going to show up here? New features, first and foremost. When something new lands in the game, I'll write a bit about what it is and why it ended up that way. The leaderboard with its weekly challenge is a good example of something that deserved a post, but it shipped before this page existed.

Then there are changes. When I tweak the numbers or change how something works, you'll hear about it here. That way you won't have to wonder why the strategy that worked so well last week suddenly goes straight to bankruptcy.

And finally, usage stats! I think it's genuinely fun to see how people actually play. How many make it through all 40 quarters, which moves pay off, and how many crash and burn as early as 2028. The numbers only come from those of you who said yes to anonymous analytics, so it'll be trends and totals, never individuals.
The plan is to post regularly, and at least whenever there's something to report. Got a wish, or found a bug? Send me an email. The address is under “About”.
And… that's all I've got this time. Good luck with your quarters, and don't get burned in the backroom. Cheers!
